newsitem.title: HUNGARY: MORE GREET JACKSON THAN POPE AT BUDAPEST AIRPORT.
newsitem.headline: MORE GREET JACKSON THAN POPE AT BUDAPEST AIRPORT.

text.p: Michael Jackson arrived in Budapest on the second stage of his first tour for two years to a welcome which police said outdid the Pope's recent visit.

A crowd of over 4,000 screamed Jackson's name as he descended the steps of his silver and white Boeing 707 and walked towards them, dressed in his familiar black wide-rimmed hat and sunglasses and sporting a long black overcoat against the unseasonally cold weather
"I love it here," he told Reuters as he strolled across the tarmac. "I love these people."
Police said the crowd greeting Jackson was the largest they'd seen at the airport for years. "There were at least twice as many people here as for the Pope," said one policemen.
Pope John Paul completed a two-day visit to Hungary on Saturday.
Nine-year-old Zsofi Horvath was one of nine fans picked out from the crowd to greet Jackson at the steps of his plane. She was pushed forward to greet him but appeared too shy to shake his hand.
"He didn't say anything but it was really nice to be so close," she told Reuters.
Fans Timea Horai and Andrea Szabo had spent a week preparing a gigantic banner with the words "We care about you, Michael" in English.
Fourteen-year-old Szabo said she didn't care what the papers wrote about her hero.
"It's up to him what he does in his private life," she said. "He's just fantastic on stage,"

Fans swarmed over the smoked glass windows of his car as it inched its way out of the airport, Jackson occasionally popping up out of the open sunroof to a chorus of screams before quickly diving back in.
The cavalcade then drove to his hotel, where hundreds more waiting fans were rewarded minutes after his arrival with an appearance and a wave from his open top-floor window.
Jackson launched his first concert tour in three years on Saturday with a high-tech spectacle in Prague aimed at restoring the gleem to a career tarnished by allegations of child molestation.
As if to confront his accusers head-on, children are playing an important role in the publicity for Tuesday's Budapest concert. Later on Sunday he will have dinner with another 100 young fans.
The Hungarian organisers said all the children selected would be "hygienic and aesthetically pleasing".

Twenty-nine 30-tonne trucks have brought equipment from Prague -- eight for the stage alone, organisers said. A team of 250 people are taking three days to prepare the venue for Tuesday's concert, the 60,000-capacity People's Stadium.
The three-month "HIStory World Tour" will take hundreds of tonnes of equipment to stops in Europe, Africa, Asia, but with no dates scheduled for the Americas.

The first part of the tour has a heavy Eastern European flavour with stops planned for Hungary, Romania, Poland, and Russia, matching a theme running through his latest album "HIStory" which includes the song "Stranger in Moscow".

The first tour of the self-proclaimed "King of Pop" since 1993's "Dangerous" tour is to back Jackson's "HIStory" album which has lagged well behind his 1982 album "Thriller", the all-time top seller with 44 million copies sold worldwide.
But the tour marks his biggest effort yet to get Jackson's career back on track after a long-running scandal over child-sex abuse allegations.
The charges first came to light in August 1993, when a 13-year-old boy accused Jackson of molesting him.
Jackson denied wrongdoing but reached a multimillion-dollar settlement with the boy, and prosecutors dropped their investigation in 1994 after the child refused to testify.
